items.title: A bullet stuck in a block loses more energy than people think
items.claim: A 10 g bullet at 500 m/s embeds in a 1 kg block initially at rest. Momentum is conserved. About 99 percent of the original kinetic energy is gone — converted to heat and deformation.
items.prompt: What proportion of the initial kinetic energy is retained as KE of the bullet-and-block system?

options.text: 50 percent — half is always lost in collisions
About 1 percent — momentum and kinetic energy are separate conservation conditions; only the former is required in inelastic collisions
Energy is lost only if the block is destroyed

items.reveal_title: Momentum is always conserved; kinetic energy is not
items.reveal:
Initial momentum: 0.01 times 500 = 5 kg m/s. After embedding: (1.01) times v = 5, so v is about 4.95 m/s.
Initial KE: 0.5 times 0.01 times 500 squared = 1250 J.
Final KE: 0.5 times 1.01 times 4.95 squared = 12.4 J.

Almost all the kinetic energy has been lost — to heat, sound, deformation. About 1 percent of the bullet's original KE remains as bulk motion of the combined system.

The mass ratio matters: a bullet hitting a much heavier block loses more KE than the same bullet hitting a similar-mass block, because the velocity afterwards is much smaller.
items.why: Conservation of momentum is treated as if it also implied conservation of kinetic energy. It doesn't — only elastic collisions conserve both.

items.title: A tiny push, repeatedly, can destroy a bridge
items.claim: In November 1940, mild crosswinds of about 19 m/s set the Tacoma Narrows Bridge into a torsional oscillation. Within hours, the deck twisted itself apart and collapsed. The wind force was modest. The destruction wasn't.
items.prompt: Why was a steady wind so devastating?

options.text: The wind was much stronger than reported
Aeroelastic flutter — the bridge's twisting motion modified the air flow in a way that pumped energy back into the same motion at exactly the bridge's natural frequency, amplifying every cycle
Earthquake activity coincided with the wind
Workers loosened bolts the night before

items.reveal_title: Resonance can extract energy from a steady source
items.reveal:
If energy is pumped into an oscillator at exactly its natural frequency, the amplitude grows linearly with time — even tiny forces can produce huge displacements.

The Tacoma Narrows failure wasn't simple wind-driven resonance, but aeroelastic flutter — the deck's torsional motion changed the lift on the deck in a way that drove the next cycle. A small constant wind became a destructive resonant amplifier through this feedback.

Millennium Bridge in London (2000) saw the same thing with pedestrians: walkers' small lateral footfalls synchronised with the deck's natural side-to-side mode, and the bridge wobbled wildly. The crowd unconsciously walked in step to match the resonance.
items.why: Linear thinking ('small force gives small effect') breaks at resonance. Repeated small forces at the right frequency can do unbounded work.

items.title: Heat and temperature are different things
items.claim: A burning sparkler reaches 1000°C. A cup of hot tea is at 80°C. Touching the sparkler causes no damage; touching the tea would scald you. Yet the sparkler is much hotter.
items.prompt: Why does the cooler tea cause more damage?

options.text: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy per particle; heat (energy transferred) depends on temperature, mass and specific heat capacity. A cup of tea has a huge total heat content compared to a few sparks of iron
Tea is more conductive than sparks

items.reveal:
A sparkler's molten iron particles are at high temperature (high kinetic energy per atom) but the total mass is tiny — a few milligrams. Total heat: 0.001 kg × 460 J/kg·K × 1000 K ≈ 0.5 J.

A cup of tea is at lower temperature but contains 250 g of water. Total heat above body temperature: 0.25 × 4180 × 40 ≈ 42,000 J — about 100,000 times more.

Damage to skin depends on how much heat is delivered before equilibrium, which depends on total heat content and contact area. A drop of liquid metal delivers a brief, intense local heating but small total energy; a cup of tea delivers sustained heat over a larger area.

This is why some materials (low specific heat capacity, low mass) feel hot to touch but don't burn you, while others (high specific heat, high mass) can scald at much lower temperatures.
items.why: Heat and temperature are often used interchangeably. They are mathematically and physically distinct quantities — and the difference matters for safety.
